name: Banzai Pipeline
seasonality: North Pacific storms send consistent W-NW groundswell from November to March; the North Shore is usually flat in summer.
accessibility_notes: Walk-in from Ehukai Beach Park off Kamehameha Highway (very limited parking; TheBus serves the North Shore), then paddle out from the beach.
hazards: Shallow, uneven lava reef with caves and ledges, heavy crowds and localism; serious injuries and fatalities have occurred.
description: The world's most famous barrel: a hollow left that breaks over a series of lava reef ledges (First, Second and Third Reef) off Ehukai Beach. Backdoor, the right off the same peak, takes over on more northerly swells.

airports.notes: ~55 km via H-1, H-2 and Kamehameha Hwy; allow extra time in traffic.

name: Sunset Beach
seasonality: Best from October to March on NW-N groundswell; the West Peak bowl lights up on more westerly swells. Generally flat in summer.
accessibility_notes: Roadside parking at Sunset Beach Park on Kamehameha Highway; paddle out through the channel from the beach.
hazards: Strong currents and rips, a shifting peak that catches surfers inside, long hold-downs and a shallow inside reef.
description: A big, shifting right-hand reef peak breaking well offshore, with a steep, hollow West Peak section on west-north-west swells. Known for size, power and long rides, it is a proving ground for big-wall surfing.

airports.notes: ~60 km via H-1, H-2 and Kamehameha Hwy.

name: Waimea Bay
seasonality: The outer reef only breaks properly on the largest NW-NNW winter swells, typically a handful of days per season between December and February.
accessibility_notes: Waimea Bay Beach Park off Kamehameha Highway; the car park fills early on big days. Paddle out from the beach, timing the shorebreak.
hazards: Giant waves with long hold-downs, a dangerous shorebreak and strong currents across the bay; experienced big-wave surfers only.
description: A historic big-wave arena where the reef off the bay's northeast point starts breaking properly at roughly 20 ft faces. It hosts the Eddie Aikau invitational, which runs only when waves hold a consistent 20 ft Hawaiian scale (roughly 35-40 ft faces).

airports.notes: ~50 km via H-1, H-2 and Kamehameha Hwy.

name: Jaws (Peʻahi)
seasonality: Breaks on large NW-N North Pacific groundswells between November and March; it needs long-period swell to come alive.
accessibility_notes: No public road to the lineup. Surfers launch jet skis from the Maliko Gulch boat ramp or paddle out from the boulder shore; spectators reach the clifftop over dirt roads through private farmland, and access may be restricted.
hazards: Giant waves, lethal hold-downs, a boulder-lined shore with no safe exit and heavy jet-ski traffic; water safety teams are essential.
description: One of the world's premier big-wave reefs, where a deep-water reef ridge focuses North Pacific swell into giant, clean rights and lefts. Originally a tow-in arena, it is now also paddled at 30-60 ft faces.

airports.notes: ~20 km east via the Hana Hwy (HI-36) through Paia.
Inter-island flight HNL-OGG (~40 min), then drive.

name: Mavericks
region: Pillar Point, Half Moon Bay, California
seasonality: Big-wave season runs from November to March, when large, long-period W-NW swells arrive from North Pacific storms.
accessibility_notes: Walk about 20-30 min from the Pillar Point Harbor / Pillar Point Bluff parking past the radar station, then a long paddle (~1 km); many surfers launch by boat or jet ski from Pillar Point Harbor.
hazards: Cold water (about 10-13 °C), giant waves, rocks on the inside ('the Boneyard'), strong currents and sharks; several fatalities, including Mark Foo in 1994.
description: A cold-water big-wave reef about 1 km off Pillar Point, where a sloping rock reef focuses deep-water W-NW swell into giant, heavy rights (with occasional lefts). Holds 25-50 ft faces on strong winter swells.

airports.notes: ~40 km via I-280 and CA-92 or along CA-1.
~75 km via I-280/CA-92.
~55 km via the San Mateo Bridge and CA-92.

name: Ocean Beach (San Francisco)
seasonality: Autumn (September-November) brings the first NW groundswells and the most offshore days; winter is bigger and often maxed out, while spring and summer bring NW wind and fog.
accessibility_notes: Drive or take Muni (N-Judah / L-Taraval) to the Great Highway; park along the beach and walk across the sand.
hazards: Powerful rip currents, very difficult paddle-outs on big days, cold water and shifting sandbars.
description: A 5.5 km stretch of exposed beach break along San Francisco's western edge with fast, heavy, cold-water peaks. Shape depends on the sandbars, and at size it is one of the most difficult paddle-outs in California.

airports.notes: ~25 km via I-280 / CA-1.
~40 km via the Bay Bridge.

name: Trestles (Lower Trestles)
region: San Onofre State Beach, San Clemente, California
seasonality: Best from late spring to autumn when S-SSW Southern Hemisphere groundswells and Mexican hurricane swells arrive; winter W-NW swells are partly blocked.
accessibility_notes: Park at the Trestles trailhead (Cristianitos Rd / El Camino Real, state-park parking fee) and walk about 1.5 km (20-30 min) through San Onofre State Beach and under the railroad trestle to the beach.
hazards: Extreme crowds and a cobblestone bottom; rattlesnakes in the brush along the trail.
description: A cobblestone peak at the mouth of San Mateo Creek producing high-performance rights and lefts, widely regarded as California's most consistent quality summer wave. It has hosted the WSL Finals and many other professional contests.

airports.notes: ~50 km south on I-5, then a 20-30 min walk in.
~95 km north on I-5, then a 20-30 min walk in.
~110 km via I-405 and I-5, then a 20-30 min walk in; traffic-dependent.

name: Rincon Point
region: Santa Barbara / Ventura county line, California
seasonality: A winter spot: it needs W-WNW groundswell squeezing between the Channel Islands, usually from November to March, and is mostly flat in summer.
accessibility_notes: Park at the Rincon Beach Park / Bates Road lots just off US-101 and walk to the Cove; parking is limited.
hazards: Heavy crowds, cobblestones and rocks, and poor water quality after rain from creek runoff.
description: The 'Queen of the Coast': a long cobblestone right point that can link from the Indicator through the Rivermouth to the Cove on winter WNW swells. The Channel Islands shelter it, so it needs solid west swell, but it rewards it with long, tapering walls.

airports.notes: ~30 km east on US-101.
~140 km north-west on US-101; traffic-dependent.

name: Puerto Escondido (Zicatela)
seasonality: Peak season is April to September, when S-SW Southern Hemisphere swells and tropical storms produce the biggest, hollowest days; winter is smaller but still gets surf.
accessibility_notes: Short taxi ride from Puerto Escondido airport to Zicatela, where hotels line the beach; walk in and paddle out from the sand.
hazards: Extremely powerful closeouts and shorebreak, frequent broken boards and strong rips; lifeguards perform many rescues.
description: The 'Mexican Pipeline': a heavy, hollow beach break where a deep offshore canyon funnels Pacific swell onto a steep sand bottom. It produces thick barrels from head-high to well over double overhead.

airports.notes: ~5 km by taxi.
~4-6 h by road depending on route; a new highway opened in 2024 shortens the trip. Most travellers connect by air to PXM instead.
Domestic flight MEX-PXM (~1 h), then a short taxi.

name: Punta de Lobos
seasonality: Surf runs year-round; the biggest S-SW swells arrive from March to October (austral autumn and winter), while summer is smaller with afternoon southerly winds.
accessibility_notes: About 6 km (10 min) south of Pichilemu; park on the headland, take the steep path down, then jump off the rocks by the sea stacks or paddle from the beach.
hazards: Cold water (about 12-15 °C), a rocky entry and exit around the sea stacks, strong currents and heavy big-wave days.
description: A long, powerful left point that wraps around a rocky headland marked by two sea stacks (Los Morros), holding swell from about 4 ft to 40 ft+ faces. It is one of South America's best-known waves and a big-wave contest venue.

airports.notes: ~230 km south-west via Routes 78 and 66 to Pichilemu.

name: Chicama (Puerto Malabrigo)
seasonality: Best from March to October, when large, long-period S-SW swells from austral autumn and winter storms wrap along the point.
accessibility_notes: About 75 km (75 min) north of Trujillo via the Panamericana Norte and the Paiján turnoff; local boat tow-back services from the pier help surfers ride several sections.
hazards: Cold water, strong currents running along the point, very long walks or paddles back, and pollution near the pier.
description: One of the world's longest left-hand point breaks, peeling over sand-covered rock sections (Malpaso, El Cape, El Point, El Hombre) that can link for well over 1 km on solid SW swells. It is protected under Peru's surf-break preservation law.

airports.notes: ~75 km north via the Panamericana Norte.
Domestic flight LIM-TRU (~1 h 10 min), then drive.

name: Lobitos
seasonality: Gets swell year-round; S-SW swells from March to October are the most consistent, and northern-winter NW swells add variety from December to February.
accessibility_notes: About 18 km (25 min) north of Talara on paved and dirt roads (4x4 helpful for some breaks); accommodation in the village is within walking distance of the waves.
hazards: Sand-covered rock and reef, old oil-industry piers and pipes, strong currents; robberies of surfers have been reported on the road from Talara.
description: A desert-backed left point with several setups (Lobitos, El Hueco, Piscinas, Generales) producing long, fast, often hollow lefts. Strong, near-constant offshore winds groom the waves most of the year.

airports.notes: ~20 km north of Talara.
~140 km via Sullana and Talara.

name: Uluwatu
seasonality: Dry season (April-October) brings consistent SW Indian Ocean groundswell with ESE-SE trade winds blowing offshore; the wet season brings onshore westerlies.
accessibility_notes: Drive to the clifftop warungs at Uluwatu (Suluban), take the stairs down through the cave and paddle out from the cave mouth.
hazards: Shallow, sharp reef, strong currents that can sweep surfers past the cave exit, and crowds.
description: Bali's most famous wave: a long, powerful left breaking along a limestone reef below the cliffs, with distinct sections (Racetracks, the Peak, Outside Corner, Temples). It holds swell from about 3 ft to 15 ft+ faces.

airports.notes: ~20 km south onto the Bukit; allow extra for traffic.

name: Padang Padang
seasonality: Only breaks properly on solid SW groundswells during the dry season (roughly May-September), a limited number of days each year.
accessibility_notes: Park near the Padang Padang bridge on Jalan Labuansait and walk down the steps through a rock crevice to the beach, then paddle out.
hazards: Extremely shallow, sharp reef under a heavy, hollow barrel, and intense crowds when it breaks.
description: The 'Balinese Pipeline': a short, heavy, hollow left breaking over a shallow reef ledge on big SW swells. It comes alive only a limited number of days each dry season and hosts the Rip Curl Cup Padang Padang.

airports.notes: ~18 km south onto the Bukit; allow extra for traffic.

name: Keramas
seasonality: Best in the wet season (November-March), when W-NW monsoon winds blow offshore; in the dry season it is surfed early in the morning before the trade winds turn onshore.
accessibility_notes: About 45 min from the airport via the Ida Bagus Mantra bypass; park at the beach and paddle out from the black-sand shore.
hazards: Shallow volcanic reef, crowds and strong onshore winds by late morning in the dry season.
description: A fast, hollow, high-performance right over shallow volcanic reef on Bali's east coast. It has hosted WSL Championship Tour events.

airports.notes: ~30 km via the Ida Bagus Mantra bypass.

name: Desert Point (Bangko-Bangko)
region: Sekotong, southwest Lombok, West Nusa Tenggara
seasonality: Needs large, long-period SW swells and dry-season SE trades, which come mainly from May to September; it can be flat for weeks between swells.
accessibility_notes: Remote: about 2.5-3 h drive from Lombok airport over rough roads, or by fast boat or charter from Bali. Basic accommodation at the point.
hazards: Very shallow, sharp reef, fast hollow sections, strong currents and a remote location with limited medical help.
description: A world-class, very long and hollow left that wraps along a shallow reef into the Lombok Strait, offering multiple barrels per ride on big SW swells. It is inconsistent and needs the right combination of swell, tide and trade winds.

airports.notes: ~90 km via Lembar and Sekotong; the last section is rough road.
Fast boat or charter from Bali to the point or to Lembar, then road transfer.

name: G-Land (Grajagan / Plengkung)
region: Alas Purwo National Park, Banyuwangi, East Java
seasonality: Dry season (April-October) brings consistent SSW-SW groundswell and SE trade winds blowing offshore; the surf camps operate mainly in this window.
accessibility_notes: Reached via surf camps inside Alas Purwo National Park: drive to Grajagan harbour, then about 1 h by boat. Packages from Bali include the transfer.
hazards: Shallow, sharp reef (especially Speedies at low tide), strong currents and a remote jungle location.
description: A long left reef with distinct sections (Kongs, Moneytrees, Launching Pads and the fast, hollow Speedies) fronting a jungle-covered national park. It is among the longest and most consistent world-class lefts in Indonesia.

airports.notes: ~1.5 h drive to Grajagan harbour, then ~1 h boat to the surf camps.
Drive ~3.5 h to Gilimanuk, take the ferry to Ketapang (Java), drive to Grajagan, then boat to camp; camps arrange the whole transfer.

name: Lakey Peak
region: Hu'u, Dompu, Sumbawa, West Nusa Tenggara
seasonality: Dry season (April-October) brings consistent SW swell; mornings are best before the trade winds pick up.
accessibility_notes: Fly to Bima, then about 2.5 h by car via Dompu to Lakey Beach in Hu'u; the peak is a short paddle from the beachfront guesthouses.
hazards: Shallow reef, crowds and strong afternoon winds.
description: A high-quality A-frame reef peak producing hollow lefts and shorter rights, the centrepiece of a cluster of breaks (Lakey Pipe, Periscopes, Nungas, Cobblestones) on Sumbawa's south coast. It is very consistent through the dry season.

airports.notes: ~2.5 h drive via Dompu to Hu'u.
Domestic flight DPS-BMU (~1 h 15 min), then ~2.5 h drive.

name: Macaronis
region: North Pagai, Mentawai Islands, West Sumatra
seasonality: Dry season (April-October) brings consistent SW Indian Ocean swell and lighter winds; outside this window the swell is less reliable and winds are variable.
accessibility_notes: Boat only: fly to Padang, then a fast ferry to Sikakap or a charter speedboat (4-5 h) to the Mentawais. Most surfers stay at the resort facing the break or on a charter yacht.
hazards: Shallow reef on the inside sections and a remote location far from medical facilities.
description: A mechanical, playful left that peels along a reef at the edge of a bay on North Pagai, offering long walls and tube sections. It is very consistent through the dry season and popular with resort guests and charter boats.

airports.notes: ~30 min to Padang port, then fast ferry to Sikakap or charter speedboat (~4-5 h); resort transfers available.

name: Rifles (Kandui Right)
region: Karangmajat Island, Playgrounds area, Mentawai Islands
seasonality: Dry season (April-October); it needs a solid SSW-SW groundswell and light NE winds, so it breaks less often than nearby Playgrounds waves.
accessibility_notes: Boat only: fly to Padang, then a fast ferry to Sipora or a charter speedboat (3-4 h) to the Playgrounds area; stay at a nearby resort or on a charter boat.
hazards: Very shallow, sharp reef under fast, hollow sections, and a remote location far from medical facilities.
description: A long, very fast and hollow right that reels down a shallow reef off Karangmajat Island, offering multiple barrel sections. It needs a solid SSW-SW swell to come alive.

airports.notes: ~30 min to Padang port, then fast ferry to Tua Pejat (Sipora) or charter speedboat (~3-4 h) to the Playgrounds.

name: Cloudbreak
seasonality: April to October brings the most consistent SW Southern Ocean groundswell, though SE trade winds can be strong; the wet season has lighter winds but less swell.
accessibility_notes: Boat only: from Tavarua or Namotu island resorts (about 10 min), or by boat from mainland bases such as Port Denarau and Wailoaloa (30-45 min). It has been open to all boats since Fiji ended surf-break exclusivity in 2010.
hazards: Shallow, sharp coral reef (especially the inside 'Shish Kebabs' section), heavy waves on big swells and a long boat ride to hospital.
description: A powerful, long left on the outer barrier reef that holds anything from about 4 ft to 20 ft+ faces, with sections such as Top of the Point, Middles and Shish Kebabs. It is regarded as one of the world's best big lefts and is a WSL Championship Tour venue.

airports.notes: ~20 min drive to Port Denarau or Wailoaloa, then a 30-45 min boat ride; island resort guests are about 10 min away.

name: Restaurants
seasonality: April to October brings consistent SW swell; its sheltered position means it often has cleaner conditions than Cloudbreak in the SE trade winds.
accessibility_notes: Breaks just off the southwest tip of Tavarua Island; reached by boat from Tavarua or from mainland and other island operators.
hazards: Very shallow, sharp coral reef with frequent reef cuts, especially at low tide.
description: A mechanical, perfectly peeling left over shallow coral off Tavarua, offering long, hollow walls. It is smaller and more forgiving than Cloudbreak and a WSL Fiji Pro venue.

airports.notes: ~30 min drive to the Uciwai landing, then ~20 min boat to Tavarua.

name: Teahupoʻo
seasonality: April to September (austral winter) brings the strongest SSW-SW Southern Ocean groundswells; it gets surf year-round but is most consistent in this period.
accessibility_notes: Drive about 1-1.5 h from Papeete to the end of the road at Teahupoʻo village, then a short boat or jet-ski ride (or a 15-20 min paddle) out through the pass to the reef.
hazards: An extremely heavy wave over very shallow live coral, potentially fatal wipeouts and strong currents in the channel.
description: One of the heaviest waves in the world: a thick, below-sea-level left that pitches over a shallow coral ledge next to the Havae pass. It hosted the surfing events of the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.

airports.notes: ~60 km (1-1.5 h) drive to the end of the road at Teahupoʻo, then a 5-10 min boat ride.

name: Shipstern Bluff
seasonality: Best from April to September, when Southern Ocean storms send large S-SW swells; light northerly winds are needed.
accessibility_notes: Remote: about 1.5 h drive from Hobart to the trailhead near Stormlea on the Tasman Peninsula, then a roughly 2 h bush hike, or by boat or jet ski from peninsula ports (around 30 km).
hazards: A ledging, stepped slab over a rock shelf, cold water, sharks and seals, and a remote location with no easy rescue.
description: A notorious right-hand slab where Southern Ocean swell hits a rock shelf below a towering bluff, producing steps and ledges across the face. It is surfed only by experienced big-wave and tow teams.

airports.notes: ~100 km (1.5 h) drive to the trailhead near Stormlea, then a ~2 h hike.

name: Bells Beach
seasonality: Autumn and winter (March-September) bring consistent SW Southern Ocean groundswell and more frequent NW offshore winds.
accessibility_notes: About 1.5 h (110 km) from Melbourne Airport via Geelong and Torquay; clifftop car park at the Bells Beach reserve with stairs down to the beach.
hazards: Cold water, rocky reef, strong rips on big days and sharks.
description: A classic right-hand reef bowl beneath limestone cliffs, with sections such as Rincon and the Bowl. It is home to the Rip Curl Pro, a contest dating back to 1962 and often cited as the world's longest-running surfing competition.

airports.notes: ~110 km via the M1 and Geelong Ring Road.
~60 km via Geelong.

name: Snapper Rocks / Superbank
seasonality: Cyclone season (January-April) brings E-NE cyclone swells and autumn adds SE groundswell; winter is smaller but cleaner.
accessibility_notes: About 10 min from Gold Coast Airport to Rainbow Bay / Snapper Rocks; limited parking at Point Danger. Jump off the rocks at Snapper or walk around from Rainbow Bay.
hazards: Extreme crowds and drop-ins, rocks at the take-off and a strong sweep along the bank.
description: A sand-bottom right point that starts at Snapper Rocks and, when sand pumped by the Tweed River bypassing system builds the Superbank, can link through Rainbow Bay and Greenmount toward Kirra for rides of over 1 km. It is a long-time WSL Championship Tour venue.

airports.notes: ~4 km.
~110 km south via the M1.

name: Kirra
seasonality: Needs a large E-SE cyclone swell or strong SE groundswell, most often from January to May; it can go months without breaking properly.
accessibility_notes: Next to Gold Coast Airport (about 5 min drive); paddle out from Kirra Beach beside the Big Groyne.
hazards: Fast, shallow sandbank barrels, heavy crowds and a strong current sweeping down the beach.
description: A fast, hollow sand-bottom right that peels down the beach from the Big Groyne at Kirra Point; on its day it is one of the world's best barrels. Its quality depends heavily on sand flow, which has varied with the Tweed River sand bypassing.

airports.notes: ~2 km.
~105 km south via the M1.

name: Burleigh Heads
seasonality: Best on E-SE cyclone swells and solid SE groundswells, mostly from January to June.
accessibility_notes: About 20 min north of Gold Coast Airport; paddle out from the beach or jump off the boulders at the headland in Burleigh Heads National Park.
hazards: Basalt boulders at entry and exit, a strong sweep along the point and crowds.
description: A powerful, hollow sand-bottom right that wraps around the basalt headland of Burleigh Heads National Park. It holds bigger swells than the other Gold Coast points.

airports.notes: ~15 km north via the Gold Coast Hwy / M1.
~90 km south via the M1.

name: The Box
region: Cape Mentelle, Margaret River, Western Australia
seasonality: Autumn (March-May) brings solid SW groundswell with frequent E offshore mornings; winter swells are bigger but often wind-affected.
accessibility_notes: Park at the Margaret River Main Break (Surfers Point) car park and walk past the river mouth onto the reef; about 3.5 h (270 km) from Perth.
hazards: An extremely shallow, square-lipped slab over a rock ledge; serious injuries are common and sharks are present in the region.
description: A short, extremely heavy right that throws a square barrel over shallow reef just north of the Margaret River mouth. It is one of Western Australia's most dangerous waves.

airports.notes: ~270 km south via the Forrest and Bussell Highways.
~60 km south.

name: Margaret River Main Break (Surfers Point)
seasonality: Gets swell year-round; autumn (March-May) is prime, with solid SW groundswell and E offshore mornings, while winter brings the biggest but stormiest swells.
accessibility_notes: Sealed road to the Surfers Point car park at Prevelly, about 10 min west of Margaret River town; paddle out from the point to the reef.
hazards: Powerful waves, long hold-downs on big days, a shallow inside reef, strong currents and sharks.
description: A powerful, open-ocean reef peak whose main wave is a long, thick left, with a shorter right off the other side of the peak. It holds 20 ft+ faces and is a long-time WSL Championship Tour venue (Margaret River Pro).

airports.notes: ~265 km south via the Forrest and Bussell Highways.
~55 km south.

name: North Point (Gracetown)
seasonality: Needs a solid SW groundswell with E winds, most reliable in autumn (March-May) and spring.
accessibility_notes: About 20 min north of Margaret River town to Gracetown; park on the clifftop above the break and climb down the rocks to jump in.
hazards: Heavy, ledging barrels over shallow rock reef, a difficult rock entry and exit, crowds, and sharks in the region.
description: A heavy, hollow right-hand reef on the north side of Cowaramup Bay that grinds along a rock ledge on solid SW swells. It is one of the region's most challenging and crowded waves.

airports.notes: ~250 km south via the Forrest and Bussell Highways.
~45 km south-west.

name: Jeffreys Bay (Supertubes)
seasonality: Austral winter (May-September) brings long-period SW groundswell from Southern Ocean lows and frequent W-NW offshore winds.
accessibility_notes: About 75 km (50-60 min) west of Gqeberha airport on the N2; Supertubes is in town, with walk-in access from the beachfront boardwalks.
hazards: Sharp rocks and urchins at entry and exit, fast, powerful waves, cold water in winter and sharks.
description: One of the world's best right-hand point breaks: a fast, hollow, mechanical wall that can link from Boneyards through Supertubes to Impossibles on solid SW groundswell. It is a long-time WSL Championship Tour venue (the J-Bay Open).

airports.notes: ~75 km west on the N2.
Domestic flight CPT-PLZ (~1 h 15 min), then drive.
Domestic flight JNB-PLZ (~1 h 40 min), then drive.

name: Dungeons
region: Hout Bay, Cape Peninsula, Western Cape
seasonality: Breaks on large SW swells from Southern Ocean cold fronts, mainly in the austral winter (May-September).
accessibility_notes: Boat or jet ski from Hout Bay Harbour (10-15 min); there is no land access to the lineup.
hazards: Giant waves, cold water (about 12 °C), kelp, rocks under the Sentinel, great white sharks and long hold-downs.
description: South Africa's premier big-wave reef, breaking about 1 km off the Sentinel at the mouth of Hout Bay, where heavy rights form on large SW swells. It hosted the Red Bull Big Wave Africa contest.

airports.notes: ~35 km drive to Hout Bay Harbour, then 10-15 min by boat or jet ski.

name: Skeleton Bay
region: Pelican Point peninsula, Walvis Bay, Erongo Region
seasonality: Breaks mainly in the austral winter (May-September) on large, long-period SSW-SW swells; the strong prevailing southerly winds blow side-offshore down the line.
accessibility_notes: 4x4 only: about 30-45 min from Walvis Bay across the salt flats and onto the Pelican Point spit; local guides or permits are recommended.
hazards: Fast, heavy barrels over shallow sand, a very strong down-the-line current that forces long walks back, cold water, sharks and seals, and a remote desert location.
description: An extraordinarily long, fast, hollow left that reels along a sand spit for well over 1 km on long-period SSW-SW swells, allowing several barrels per wave. Its shape and position migrate as the spit grows northward.

airports.notes: ~15 km to Walvis Bay, then 4x4 out onto the spit (30-45 min).
~390 km via the B2 through Swakopmund, then 4x4 onto the spit.

name: Supertubos
seasonality: Autumn through spring (September-March) brings North Atlantic groundswell; it is offshore in the prevailing northerly winds, while the north-facing beaches across the Peniche peninsula (Baleal) work in southerly winds.
accessibility_notes: About 1 h (95 km) north of Lisbon airport via the A8; the beach car park sits directly behind the break.
hazards: Heavy shorebreak barrels, strong currents and shallow sandbanks.
description: One of Europe's best beach breaks: powerful, hollow sandbar barrels on the south side of the Peniche peninsula, nicknamed the 'European Pipeline'. It is a long-time WSL Championship Tour venue.

airports.notes: ~95 km north via the A8.
~250 km south via the A1 and A8.

name: Nazaré (Praia do Norte)
seasonality: Big-wave season runs from October to March, when large W-NW North Atlantic swells are amplified by the Nazaré Canyon.
accessibility_notes: About 1.25 h (120 km) north of Lisbon via the A8; spectators watch from the Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo lighthouse. Big-wave sessions are tow-in by jet ski from Nazaré harbour.
hazards: Giant, unpredictable waves, strong currents, a heavy shorebreak and rocks below the fort.
description: Home of the largest waves ever surfed (a Guinness record of 26.21 m / 86 ft, set in 2020), where the Nazaré Canyon focuses North Atlantic swell onto Praia do Norte to create mountainous peaks. Smaller days produce powerful beach-break peaks.

airports.notes: ~120 km north via the A8.
~200 km south via the A1 and A8.

name: Coxos
seasonality: Autumn and winter (October-March) bring the NW-NNW groundswells it needs; it is mostly flat in summer.
accessibility_notes: About 45 min (50 km) from Lisbon airport; small dirt car park above the bay at Ribamar, then walk down and paddle out or jump off the rocks.
hazards: Shallow rock reef, strong currents and rips, heavy sets, crowds and localism.
description: Ericeira's most powerful wave: a heavy, hollow right breaking over a rock reef in a small bay, with long walls and barrels on NW groundswell. It is part of the Ericeira World Surfing Reserve.

airports.notes: ~50 km north-west via the A8 and A21.

name: Mundaka
seasonality: Works on large NW groundswells from October to March, best at low tide; the quality varies year to year with the shape of the sandbar.
accessibility_notes: About 40 min (40 km) from Bilbao airport; park in Mundaka village and paddle out from the harbour.
hazards: Strong tidal currents in the estuary, a shallow sandbar, crowds and localism.
description: Europe's most famous left: a long, hollow rivermouth wave peeling along a sandbar at the mouth of the Urdaibai (Oka) estuary. It needs a big NW swell and a well-formed sandbar to fire.

airports.notes: ~40 km via Mungia and Bermeo.
~150 km via the AP-8.

name: Hossegor (La Gravière)
seasonality: Autumn (September-November) is prime, with W-NW Atlantic groundswell and frequent E offshore winds; winter is bigger and stormier.
accessibility_notes: About 35 min (35 km) north of Biarritz airport via the A63; park along the Hossegor seafront and walk onto the beach.
hazards: Heavy, thick barrels and shorebreak, strong rips and shifting sandbars; broken boards are common.
description: The heaviest of Hossegor's beach breaks: thick, hollow peaks powered by deep water from the nearby Gouf de Capbreton submarine canyon. It is a long-time venue of the Quiksilver Pro France.

airports.notes: ~35 km north via the A63.
~170 km south via the A63.

name: Anchor Point
seasonality: North Atlantic NW groundswells and NE offshore winds make October to March the main season; summer is small and windy.
accessibility_notes: About 40 km (40 min) north of Agadir airport on the N1 coast road; park by the road just north of Taghazout village and walk to the point.
hazards: A rocky point with sea urchins, a tricky entry and exit off the rocks, and crowds.
description: Morocco's best-known right point: long, walling rights that can run several hundred metres along a rocky point on solid NW swell. It is the centrepiece of the Taghazout surf scene.

airports.notes: ~40 km north via Agadir and the N1.
~250 km via the A7 motorway and N1.

name: Safi (Le Jardin)
seasonality: Needs a large NW groundswell, so it works mainly from November to March and only on bigger swells.
accessibility_notes: On the northern edge of Safi; park on the clifftop and climb down to the rocks to paddle out. About 2 h by road from Marrakech.
hazards: Heavy, hollow barrels, rocks, strong currents and a difficult entry and exit; locals can be territorial.
description: A world-class, hollow right point that breaks fast and long over sand and rock on big NW swells, regarded as one of Africa's best barrels. It only starts working on larger swells, mainly in winter.

airports.notes: ~160 km west via the R207.
~250 km south via the A1 / A5 coastal motorway.

name: Punta Roca
seasonality: Most consistent from April to October, when S-SSW Southern Hemisphere groundswells arrive; the dry season (November-March) brings smaller swell and steady offshore winds.
accessibility_notes: At the western edge of La Libertad town; walk in through the point access and paddle out off the boulders.
hazards: Boulder and rock bottom, sea urchins, pollution after rain from the town and river, and crowds.
description: El Salvador's best-known wave: a long, powerful right that peels over a boulder point at La Libertad. It has hosted WSL Championship Tour events (Surf City El Salvador Pro).

airports.notes: ~40 km west along the coastal highway (CA-2).

name: Pavones
seasonality: Works best in the rainy season (April-September) on long-period S swells from the Southern Hemisphere; it is flat for long stretches without the right swell angle.
accessibility_notes: Very remote: fly domestically to Golfito (or drive 7-8 h from San José), then about 1-1.5 h by road. The break is in front of the village, next to the soccer field.
hazards: Rocky, cobbled bottom, long walks or paddles back up the point, crowds on good swells and limited medical facilities nearby.
description: One of the world's longest lefts: a sand-and-cobble point at the mouth of Golfo Dulce where good south swells produce rides of several hundred metres, occasionally approaching 1 km. It is very sensitive to swell direction and is best on long-period S swells.

airports.notes: Domestic flight SJO-Golfito (GLF, ~1 h), then ~1-1.5 h by road; or ~7-8 h drive.
~45 km via Conte and the coastal road (partly unpaved).

name: Salsa Brava
region: Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, Limón Province
seasonality: Caribbean swells from winter cold fronts and strong trade winds make December to March the main season; it is often flat the rest of the year.
accessibility_notes: Breaks right in front of Puerto Viejo village; paddle out from the beach in town. About 4.5 h by road from San José.
hazards: Very shallow, sharp coral reef, heavy hollow sections and strong localism.
description: A heavy, hollow right (with a shorter left) that throws thick barrels over shallow coral in front of Puerto Viejo on NE-E swells. It is the best-known wave on Costa Rica's Caribbean coast.

airports.notes: ~210 km via Route 32 through Braulio Carrillo and Limón.
~60 km south via Route 36; scheduled service at Limón is limited, so check current schedules.

name: Playa Hermosa (Jacó)
seasonality: Surf runs year-round, but the April-October rainy season brings the most consistent S-SW groundswell; mornings are usually glassy or offshore.
accessibility_notes: About 5 km south of Jacó on the Costanera (Route 34); several beach access paths lead to the peaks along the black-sand beach.
hazards: Powerful closeouts, strong rip currents and occasional crocodiles near river mouths.
description: A consistent, powerful black-sand beach break with many peaks along an 8 km stretch south of Jacó. It is a World Surfing Reserve and a regular contest venue.

airports.notes: ~100 km via Route 27.
~230 km via Route 1, Route 23 and Route 34.

name: Bocas del Toro (Silverbacks)
region: Isla Bastimentos, Bocas del Toro Archipelago
seasonality: Only breaks properly on the strongest Caribbean winter swells (roughly December to March) generated by cold fronts and strong trade winds.
accessibility_notes: Boat only: a 15-20 min water taxi from Bocas Town (Isla Colón) to the reef off the northwest tip of Isla Bastimentos.
hazards: Thick, heavy waves over shallow reef, strong currents and a remote, boat-access-only lineup.
description: A big, powerful right-hand reef off Isla Bastimentos that comes alive on large N-NE Caribbean swells, often compared to Hawaiian outer reefs. It holds waves up to about 20 ft faces.

airports.notes: Short taxi or walk to the Bocas Town docks, then a 15-20 min water taxi.
Domestic flight Panama City-Bocas del Toro (~1 h; mostly from Albrook PAC rather than Tocumen), then taxi and water taxi.

name: Cloud 9
region: General Luna, Siargao Island, Surigao del Norte
seasonality: August to November brings typhoon swells from the Philippine Sea with SW (habagat) winds blowing offshore; the NE monsoon (December-March) brings bigger but often onshore surf.
accessibility_notes: About 30-45 min from Sayak Airport to General Luna; walk along the boardwalk to the viewing tower and paddle out to the reef.
hazards: Very shallow live-coral reef with urchins, heavy crowds and typhoon-season weather.
description: A thick, hollow right (with a shorter left) at the end of a wooden boardwalk in General Luna, the Philippines' best-known wave. Typhoon swells produce powerful barrels, and it hosts an annual international surfing competition.

airports.notes: ~25 km via Dapa to General Luna.
Domestic flight CEB-IAO (~1 h), then drive.
Domestic flight MNL-IAO (~1 h 45 min), then drive.

name: Thurso East
seasonality: Autumn through spring (September-April) brings N-NW North Atlantic swells; winter days are short and cold.
accessibility_notes: On the east side of the Thurso River mouth; walk across the field near the castle ruins to the reef. About 2.5 h (175 km) north of Inverness airport.
hazards: Cold water (about 8-12 °C), sharp flagstone reef, dark peaty river water that hides the bottom, and strong currents.
description: A world-class right reef breaking over flat flagstone slabs at the mouth of the Thurso River, producing long walls and hollow sections on N-NW swells. It is widely considered the best reef break in Britain.

airports.notes: ~175 km north via the A9.
~35 km west; scheduled service at Wick is limited or intermittent, so check current schedules.

name: Raglan (Manu Bay)
seasonality: Autumn and winter (March-October) bring the most consistent SW Tasman Sea and Southern Ocean swells; summer is smaller.
accessibility_notes: About 2 h (160 km) from Auckland Airport via SH1, Hamilton and SH23, then 8 km west of Raglan town on Wainui Road; paddle out from the rocks below the car park.
hazards: Boulder and rock bottom, a difficult entry and exit on the rocks, and crowds.
description: A long, consistent left point peeling over boulders, made famous by the 1966 film The Endless Summer. It is one of a series of lefts (Manu Bay, Whale Bay, Indicators) that can connect on big SW swells.

airports.notes: ~160 km via SH1, Hamilton and SH23.
~55 km via SH23.

name: Mullaghmore Head
seasonality: Breaks on large W-NW North Atlantic winter swells (October-March), ideally with light SE offshore winds.
accessibility_notes: About 1.25 h (85 km) from Ireland West Airport Knock; park on the verge of the coast road around Mullaghmore Head. Tow teams launch from Mullaghmore harbour; paddling out from the rocks takes about 30 min.
hazards: Giant waves over a shallow, uneven limestone reef close to rocks, cold water and long hold-downs.
description: Ireland's premier big-wave spot: a heavy left (with a shorter right) breaking over a shallow limestone reef off Mullaghmore Head on big NW swells. It is surfed by tow and paddle teams during winter storms.

airports.notes: ~85 km via the N17, N4 and N15.
~220 km via the N4 and N15.
